title.text:
pandas I: load, look and filter
a table of 30,229 orders

objects.text: How do we open a file of 30,229 rows, look at it, and ask it the first questions?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 7 of 24  |  Module B: Python for data
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Until now you have worked with a few numbers and a price list. Today we open the real Lakeside Mart orders file, thirty thousand two hundred and twenty nine rows, and we start asking it questions in Python. You will load it into a pandas DataFrame, look at it before you trust it, and filter it.

Everything you do has a spreadsheet twin, and we will name it each time.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can load a CSV file into a pandas DataFrame and take a first look at it: its shape, its data types, its missing values and a summary. You can select columns and filter rows with a Boolean mask, and join two conditions.

You can sort, count and pick rows with loc and iloc. And you leave with a data profile of the Lakeside Mart orders file, saved as a small CSV that you can reuse on any file.

title.text: Your two hours: concepts first, then a pandas lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_83d54561.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the notebook. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 6 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with laptops closed, so you can follow the pictures and the real output on the slides. After a ten minute break we open a Colab notebook for a forty-five minute lab on the Lakeside Mart orders.

In every step you predict, run, read the result and change one thing. The last ten minutes are the exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  You wrote a function that gives a loyalty tier from spend. How did you test it?
2.  In Excel you drag a formula down 5,000 rows. What does a for loop do instead?
3.  What does the word return do inside a function?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 6. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. You wrote a function that gives a loyalty tier from spend. How did you test it?

A good answer is this. Run it on examples whose answer you already know, including the values exactly on each tier boundary.

Question two. In Excel you drag a formula down 5,000 rows. What does a for loop do instead?

A good answer is this. It repeats the same steps once for each item in a list, so you write the step one time.

Question three. What does the word return do inside a function?

A good answer is this. It hands the result back to the code that called the function, so you can store it or print it.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

DataFrame. A table held in Python memory, with labelled rows and named columns. In Excel words: one tab of a workbook.

Series. One column of a DataFrame. It has a name, a data type and the same index as the table.

Index. The row labels down the left edge of a DataFrame. A fresh file is labelled 0, 1, 2 and so on.

Boolean mask (Boolean indexing). A column of True and False values, one per row, used to keep only the rows marked True.

Missing value (NaN). A cell with no value. pandas shows it as NaN, SQL as NULL, and Excel as a blank cell.

objects.text: A row is called a record or an observation. A column is called a variable, or a feature in machine learning.

slides.notes:
You already know every part of this from Excel, so here is the translation. A tab is a DataFrame. A column is a Series, and in statistics words it is a variable. The row numbers are the index. AutoFilter becomes Boolean indexing, which keeps the rows where a test is true.

Sort becomes sort_values, and a PivotTable count becomes value_counts. A row is a record, also called an observation, and a column is a variable, which machine learning calls a feature. Which of these six jobs do you do most often in Excel?

title.text:
read_csv turns a file into a DataFrame,
and then we look before we ask

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_7dc8bab2.png
objects.alt: read_csv turns a file into a DataFrame, and then we look before we ask

objects.text: CSV means comma-separated values. In Colab the file sits next to the notebook, so its name is enough. pd is the usual short name for the pandas library.

slides.notes:
Every pandas job starts the same way. The file is orders dot csv, a plain text file where each line is a row and commas separate the values. The function pd dot read csv reads it into memory and gives you a DataFrame. We store it under a name, here orders, and the name is ours to choose, so pick one that says what is inside.

The letters pd are the usual short name for the pandas library. Then comes the habit we practise today: look at the data before you ask it anything. What would go wrong if you skipped the looking?

title.text:
shape gives the size, and dtypes
gives the data type of every column

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_console_11.90x4.25_332fe516.png
objects.alt: shape gives the size, and dtypes gives the data type of every column

objects.text: A data type is how a column stores its values. Session 8 converts the dates.

slides.notes:
Now two quick looks. The attribute shape gives rows first, then columns: 30,229 by 7. It is an attribute, a fact stored on the table, so it has no round brackets. Next, dtypes lists the data type of every column. Python calls text object, which pandas 3 and later shows as str, and whole numbers int64.

Notice that order_date says object. The dates are stored as text, so Python cannot yet sort them as dates or take their month. We fix that in Session 8. And promo_week is a whole number that only holds zero or one. Which other column here is text?

title.text:
info lists each column with how many
values are filled, and customer_id is short

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_console_11.90x4.25_2f4bafd2.png
objects.alt: info lists each column with how many values are filled, and customer_id is short

objects.text: info is a method: it has round brackets. Non-null means "not missing".

slides.notes:
The method info gives the table card of a DataFrame. For every column it shows the count of cells that hold a value, called the non-null count, and the data type. The table has 30,229 entries. Six columns are full. But customer_id has only 21,058 values, so the rest are missing.

That is the first thing a good analyst spots. Notice that info is a method, so it has round brackets, and shape was an attribute, so it did not. What does the last line before memory usage tell you about the file?

title.text:
isna().sum() counts the missing values, and
30 percent of orders have no customer_id

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_console_7.70x4.80_2dba348c.png
objects.alt: isna().sum() counts the missing values, and 30 percent of orders have no customer_id

objects.text: A missing value (NaN) is a cell with no value. 9,171 orders have no customer_id.

runs.text: isna() marks each empty cell True. sum() adds the Trues.
Ask what the blank means. Here it is a walk-in shopper.
Do not delete 30 percent of the orders.

slides.notes:
To count the missing values, chain two calls. isna marks every empty cell as True, and sum adds the Trues for each column. The answer: 9,171 orders have no customer id, which is 30.3 percent. Remember Session 2: the data dictionary says a blank customer id is a walk-in, a shopper with no loyalty number.

So the blank carries information, and deleting those rows would throw away three orders in ten. In pandas this blank is shown as NaN, short for not a number. Where have you seen blanks that mean something in your own files?

title.text:
describe summarises a numeric variable,
and the mean is 2.05 times the median

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_console_11.90x4.25_ced696f0.png
objects.alt: describe summarises a numeric variable, and the mean is 2.05 times the median

objects.text: A few very large orders pull the mean above the median: the variable is right-skewed.

slides.notes:
The method describe summarises a numeric variable. Count is the number of values. The mean is 47,491 shillings, the sum divided by the count. The line marked fifty percent is the median, 23,200, the middle value: half the orders are smaller. The mean is 2.05 times the median, because a few very large orders pull it up.

Statisticians call that a right-skewed variable. The largest order is 3,104,000 shillings. So which number would you quote as the typical order, the mean or the median?

objects.text: A whole-number column that has a missing value becomes float64, because NaN is a float.

slides.notes:
A table of the data types you will meet. Object holds text. Int64 holds whole numbers, like promo week and the order value. Float64 holds numbers with decimals, and also any number column that has a missing value, because NaN is stored as a float. You will see that in the loans file, where monthly income has blanks.

Bool holds True and False, which is what a mask is made of. And datetime64 holds real dates, which we create in Session 8. Remember that the data type is how the cell stores a value. The variable type, numeric or categorical, is how it is measured. Which type surprised you?

title.text:
The first look at any file: five
calls before any question

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_153abfc7.png
objects.alt: The first look at any file: five calls before any question

objects.text: This routine is the start of exploratory data analysis (EDA): getting to know a dataset before you answer questions with it.

slides.notes:
Here is the routine you will use on every new file for the rest of your career. First, shape: how many rows and columns. Second, dtypes: is each column stored as the right type. Third, head: do the first rows look sensible. Fourth, isna and sum: what is missing.

Fifth, describe: are the numbers plausible, with a sensible minimum and maximum. It takes about a minute and it catches most of the surprises. This whole habit is called exploratory data analysis, or EDA. Which of the five would have warned you about the dates?

title.text:
One column name returns a Series, and
a list of names returns a DataFrame

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_console_11.90x4.25_f541b2eb.png
objects.alt: One column name returns a Series, and a list of names returns a DataFrame

objects.text: Selecting columns is like hiding the other columns in Excel. head(3) keeps three rows.

slides.notes:
Selecting columns. Put one column name inside square brackets and you get a Series, one column with its index. Put a list of names, which means a second pair of square brackets inside the first, and you get a smaller DataFrame. That is why you see double brackets in so much pandas code: the outer pair is the selection, and the inner pair is the list.

Both outputs here are cut to three rows with head. The last line of the Series output gives its name and data type. Which would you use to get just the order values?

title.text:
A Boolean mask is a column of True and
False that chooses the rows to keep

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_mask_11.90x4.25_aa5cd4f9.png
objects.alt: A Boolean mask is a column of True and False that chooses the rows to keep

objects.text: The test builds the mask. The mask in square brackets after orders keeps the True rows.

slides.notes:
This is the idea behind every filter. Step one: we have the rows. Step two: a test, branch id equals B04, is applied to every row, and it produces a mask, a column of True and False with one value per row. A Boolean is a value that is only ever True or False.

Step three: pandas keeps only the rows where the mask is True. This is Boolean indexing, and it is what AutoFilter does for you behind the scenes. Look at the index on the right: the kept rows keep their old labels. We come back to that. Why are the first four rows False?

title.text:
Filter, count and look: 3,562
orders were sold at Jinja

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_console_11.90x4.25_97c28446.png
objects.alt: Filter, count and look: 3,562 orders were sold at Jinja

objects.text: B04 is the Jinja branch. value_counts counts each different value of a Series, like a PivotTable count.

slides.notes:
Now a real filter. We keep the orders where branch id is B04, the Jinja branch, and store them in a new DataFrame called jinja. The function len gives the number of rows, 3,562. Always write that row count beside any figure you report from a filtered table.

Then value counts on the payment method column counts each different value, like a PivotTable count. At Jinja, Mobile money leads with 1,695 orders, then cash and card. Does Mobile money lead across all branches too?

title.text:
value_counts on all 30,229 orders shows
Mobile money and cash nearly level

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_bars_7.70x4.80_033920af.png
objects.alt: value_counts on all 30,229 orders shows Mobile money and cash nearly level

objects.text: value_counts counts each different value of one variable.

runs.text: It sorts the counts from largest to smallest.
value_counts(normalize=True) returns shares instead of counts.
The three counts add up to 30,229, the number of orders.

slides.notes:
The method value counts is the pandas PivotTable count. On the whole orders file, Mobile money has 14,312 orders, cash 13,867 and card 2,050. As shares, that is 47.3, 45.9 and 6.8 percent. With the option normalize equals True you get the shares directly. A good check is that the three counts add up to 30,229, the number of orders, because every order has exactly one payment method.

What would it mean if they added to less?

title.text:
Join two conditions with &
for and, | for or and ~ for not

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_venn_11.90x4.25_cf43bd53.png
objects.alt: Join two conditions with & for and, | for or and ~ for not

objects.text: Real counts from the orders file. Circles are not to scale. Put each test in round brackets.

slides.notes:
Two conditions are two masks, and you combine them. The ampersand means and: both must be True. Jinja and Mobile money gives 1,695 orders, the gold overlap. The vertical bar means or: at least one is True. Jinja or Mobile money gives 16,179. The tilde means not: it flips every True and False, so not Mobile money gives 15,917.

The four regions add up to all 30,229 orders. In code, wrap each condition in its own round brackets. Which count would you use to find the share of Jinja orders paid by Mobile money?

title.text:
Writing and instead of &, or leaving out
the brackets, fails with a confusing error

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_console_11.90x4.25_a7b4865c.png
objects.alt: Writing and instead of &, or leaving out the brackets, fails with a confusing error

objects.text: Both errors come from running these lines. Fix: join with &, each test in round brackets.

slides.notes:
Two traps, and you will meet both. The Python word and does not work on a whole column, so pandas stops and says the truth value of a Series is ambiguous. Use the ampersand. Then the second trap: the ampersand without brackets. Python does the ampersand before the comparisons, so it tries to combine a text column with a True, and the message mentions something called rand underscore, which tells you nothing.

The fix is the same every time: put each test in its own round brackets. When you see these two messages, think brackets and ampersand. What do you do first when an error message looks strange?

title.text:
query writes the same filter as
text, and both give 1,695 orders

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_console_11.90x4.25_aa6e695e.png
objects.alt: query writes the same filter as text, and both give 1,695 orders

objects.text: Use whichever you read more easily. query is shorter when there are many conditions.

slides.notes:
Here is the same filter written two ways. The first is Boolean indexing: two masks joined with the ampersand, each in round brackets. The second uses the query method, where the whole condition is written as a piece of text. Inside that text you can write and, or, or the symbols, and you do not repeat the name of the DataFrame.

Both return 1,695 orders. Use whichever you can read more easily, and remember that the text goes in quotes inside the brackets. Which of the two would you prefer for a filter with five conditions?

title.text:
iloc counts positions and loc reads
labels, and after a filter the two differ

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_loc_iloc_11.90x4.25_8fb7cc56.png
objects.alt: iloc counts positions and loc reads labels, and after a filter the two differ

objects.text: The filter kept the old labels: position 0 is label 14060. Label 0 does not exist here.

slides.notes:
Two ways to pick rows. The attribute iloc selects by position, counting from zero. Position zero is the first row, whatever its label. The end of a slice is left out, so zero to two gives two rows. The attribute loc selects by label, the value in the index.

Here the Jinja rows kept their old labels, starting at 14060. The end of a loc slice is included, so these three labels give three rows. These two behave differently at the end, and they disagree after any filter. Use loc when you mean a label, and iloc when you mean a position.

Which would you use for the first row?

title.text:
loc and iloc take rows first, then columns,
and give the same rows on a fresh index

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_console_11.90x4.25_e69e0fda.png
objects.alt: loc and iloc take rows first, then columns, and give the same rows on a fresh index

objects.text: On a fresh index both lines return the same rows. The slice ends still behave differently.

slides.notes:
Both loc and iloc take rows first, then a comma, then columns. With loc you name the columns. With iloc you give their positions. These two lines return the same first three rows and the same first two columns. Look at the end of each slice. Loc from zero to two includes label two, so it gives three rows.

Iloc from zero to three leaves out position three, so it also gives three rows. On a fresh index the labels equal the positions, so it is easy to mix them up. The trouble starts after a filter. Which do you think is safer to read in code written by someone else?

Three habits for today and every day. First, write the row count beside any filtered result, so the reader knows how many rows a figure covers. Second, check one number a second way. In the lab you will repeat two of the filters in Google Sheets with AutoFilter.

Third, look at the mask itself: summing a mask counts its True values, so it tells you how many rows the filter will keep before you apply it. A filter that runs without an error can still be wrong, for instance with a wrong spelling or the wrong brackets.

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: ValueError: truth value of a Series is ambiguous
You wrote and or or between two tests.
Use & or |, with each test in round brackets.
You left out the round brackets around a test.
The name is misspelt or has the wrong case.
Print orders.columns and copy the name.
SyntaxError: cannot assign to subscript here. Maybe you meant '==' instead of '='?
You wrote one = where a test needs ==.
Use == to test and = to store.
The text does not match, such as b04 for B04.
Check the value with value_counts first.

slides.notes:
Five messages you may meet. The truth value of a Series is ambiguous means you wrote and or or between two tests, so use the ampersand or the bar. A type error that mentions rand underscore means you left out the round brackets. A key error is almost always a misspelt column name, so print the columns and copy.

A syntax error that suggests you meant a double equals sign means you used one equals sign where the test needs two. And a count of zero usually means the text does not match, such as a lower case b. Read the last line of the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

A DataFrame is a whole table. A Series is one column of it, with the same index.
